blocks.formula: rate of diffusion ∝ (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of the membrane

where: Doubling the surface area or the concentration difference doubles the rate.

key_idea: **Diffusion** is the spreading out of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It is how oxygen, carbon dioxide and many other substances move across cell membranes. The rate depends on the concentration gradient, temperature, surface area and distance.

blocks.text: Particles of a gas or of a substance in solution spread out. This section covers what moves and in which direction.

items.meaning: The spreading out of particles, giving a net movement from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
The difference in concentration between two places.

items: Particles move **down** a concentration gradient, from high concentration to low concentration.
Diffusion carries on until the concentrations are equal.
It does not need energy from respiration.
Particles can diffuse across cell membranes.

rows: Into cells from the blood, for respiration. In gas exchange, from the air into the blood
Out of cells into the blood. In gas exchange, from the blood into the air
Out of cells into the blood plasma, for excretion in the kidney
Glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, mineral ions

items: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move into and out of cells by diffusion.
A substance only diffuses if there is a difference in concentration.

blocks.text: Four factors change how fast a substance diffuses.

rows: More particles move down the gradient than back up it
Particles have more energy and move faster
More particles can cross at the same time
Particles have less far to travel

outputs.label: Relative rate of diffusion (a comparison, not a real measurement)

blocks.text: Keeping diffusion fast in the body

items: Gas exchange surfaces such as the alveoli are thin, one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short.
A good blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep by carrying substances away.
Ventilation brings fresh air in, which keeps the oxygen concentration high in the alveoli.
A steeper gradient, higher temperature and larger surface area all speed up diffusion.
A thicker membrane or longer distance slows diffusion down.
Exchange surfaces are thin and have a good blood supply.
